about: THE RECOMMENDED STARTUP CHAINS, AND WHY EACH ENTRY IS WHERE IT IS.
Tracked in this repository rather than written on one machine: an ordering constraint is
a fact about how these payloads work, so it is the same on every target and belongs where
it can be reviewed, corrected and versioned like anything else here.
MORE THAN ONE CHAIN, because there is more than one way to bring a PS5 up and they are not
variations on each other. A payload-manager chain loads a dozen separate payloads in an
order that matters. An etaHEN chain loads one payload that contains most of them. Advice
written for the first is wrong for the second, so they are separate presets rather than one
list with exceptions.
`order` is a rank, not an index. Lower runs earlier. Gaps are deliberate so something can
be slotted between two of these without renumbering the file.
`why` must say what *breaks* if it runs later, or state plainly that nothing does. A
payload with no ordering requirement is the normal case and says so - inventing a reason
for one would make every other line here less believable.
Names are matched the way everything else here matches them: the payload's own name, with
a version allowed on the end. `kstuff-lite` matches `kstuff-lite_v1.09.elf`.
CUSTOM PRESETS USE THEIR OWN NAMES. Shipped presets (like payload-manager) are provided and
updated by this application and cannot be overwritten by user configuration files. A `chains.json`
beside the target registry can define presets of your own using new names, which will appear
alongside the shipped presets.

A PRESET NAME IS ONE WORD. It is written on a target's line in the registry as `chain=<name>`, and that file is whitespace-delimited - so a name with a space in it would be half a name and half an address.

`result` is what a person is told they will end up with, in their words, before they agree to deploy it. The program prints it and knows nothing about what it says - so a chain added here explains itself, and one whose explanation is wrong is corrected here rather than in code.

elfldr is in the payload-manager chain ON PURPOSE and it is not there for an ordinary console. It keeps 9021 open after the boot chain has finished so payloads can be sent over the network - which is what this program is for. A console that only plays games needs none of that and is not broken for answering nothing on 9021. Take the entry out if that is your machine; the entry's own `why` explains what you lose.

`manager_order` is where an entry goes in THE MANAGER'S OWN LIST, when that is not where it goes in an autoloader's. Only the loader needs it: an autoloader's list wants it early, because it is what makes 9021 exist for everything after it, and the manager's own list wants it LAST, because everything else has already loaded by then and the point is that it is still running afterwards. One rank cannot say both.

THE `payload-manager` CHAIN IS THE CLEAN TWO-ROLE SPLIT, not a copy of one console's habits. The console this was first read from listed all its payloads in BOTH lists - so the autoloader loaded the whole chain and then the manager loaded it a second time, which works but is redundant, and it is what put an identical list at both paths. The roles are distinct and the lists should be too: the autoloader's list is only what STARTS the manager (`pldmgr`), and the manager's own list is the CHAIN it then loads, with the loader last so 9021 stays open. Everything belongs in exactly one list.

TWO FLAGS, MIRROR IMAGES. `autoloader: false` keeps an entry out of the AUTOLOADER'S list; `manager: false` keeps one out of the MANAGER'S OWN list. In the payload-manager chain every ordinary payload is `autoloader: false` and only `pldmgr` is not - because the autoloader's whole job is to start the manager, and the manager then loads the rest from its own list. `pldmgr` is `manager: false` for the plain reason that the list it reads cannot start itself. The loader was the first `autoloader: false` entry and that reason still holds independently: the y2jb autoloader loads elf_loader itself - aioshellcode.js maps and starts it, and autoload.js waits for it to answer on 9021 before reading any list - so an entry for it there is a second copy of something already running.

`lists` IS WHERE A CHAIN KEEPS ITS STARTUP LISTS, and it is here rather than in the program because it is a fact about somebody else's software that this project cannot settle and the person holding the console can. Every path the screen offers comes from this field, in some chain, in this file or in yours.

`capture` IS THE FILES A CHAIN CARRIES BESIDE ITS LIST. A chain is a payload order, but a console running it also has settings, and those are not expressible as a list of names. `capture` names the paths worth copying off a target when a chain is written down (`export chain`); an exported chain then carries a verbatim copy of each, and deploying that chain puts them back exactly. It is top-level, not per-chain, because a chain being exported is being read off a console that may match no preset here. This declares PATHS only - no machine's settings are shipped, the copies live only in chains people export. `{device}`/`{usb}` expand the same way they do for a list.
`{device}` stands for a removable device's mount point and is expanded over every one a target can have - /mnt/usb0 to /mnt/usb7 and /mnt/ext0 to /mnt/ext1. Write the stick once.
`editable` LEFT OFF MEANS READ ONLY. A list on removable storage is the way back in when the internal setup is broken, so a chain has to say so deliberately before this program will write to one.

A PLDMGR CHAIN HAS TWO LISTS AND THEY ARE NOT ALTERNATIVES. The autoloader's list starts the manager; the manager then runs ITS OWN list, at a path compiled into it - AUTOLOAD_CONFIG_PATH /data/pldmgr/autoload.txt, read from its source, one path with no removable variant. Deploying such a chain writes both.

THE AUTOLOADER'S PATHS ARE READ FROM ITS SOURCE, not from its README. find_autoload_config in itsPLK/ps5-unified-autoloader/src/main.c composes them as <base>/ps5_autoloader/autoload.txt, over /mnt/usb0 to /mnt/usb7 in order and then /data as a fallback. The y2jb repository itself never reads autoload.txt - its JavaScript loads one binary, ps5-unified-autoloader.elf, and that binary is where all of this lives.

IT SEARCHES USB STICKS ONLY. /mnt/ext0 and /mnt/ext1 are not in USB_BASES, so `{usb}` is the placeholder here rather than `{device}` - offering a path on an external drive would be offering a file nothing will ever read.

A TITLE-ID CONFIG WINS OVER ALL OF THESE. The same function looks first for <base>/ps5_autoloader_<TITLEID>/autoload.txt, where the id is whichever application was the entry point. That is not listed here because this program does not know which application launched the jailbreak; add the path yourself if you use one.

WITH NO CONFIG AT ALL, PAYLOAD MANAGER STARTS ANYWAY. From y2jb's README: "If no autoload.txt config is found, the autoloader will automatically launch Payload Manager", and "When an autoload.txt config is found, Payload Manager is not launched automatically." So a list that exists and does not name the manager is the one dangerous case, and it is the case this program audits.

AN ENTRY THAT IS NOT AN ABSOLUTE PATH RESOLVES AGAINST THE CONFIG'S OWN DIRECTORY - `snprintf(full_path, ..., "%s%s", config_dir, line)`. Payloads named in autoload.txt live beside it, so deploying a chain to a stick puts the files in the same ps5_autoloader directory as the list.

required_for_prosperous.name: kstuff-lite
required_for_prosperous.why: patches the kernel so unsigned code can run, and goes first because until it has, memory cannot be made executable and non-payload homebrew and fake packages are unavailable - measured in etaHEN's own loader, which waits for an RWX mprotect to succeed before continuing.

required_for_prosperous.name: pltauth-patch
required_for_prosperous.why: patches /dev/pltauth so native Prospero (category 0) homebrew passes PFAuthClient entitlement verification (0x80de0051). Must run after kstuff-lite so kernel memory is accessible, and before any native application launches.

required_for_prosperous.name: sandbox-daemon
required_for_prosperous.why: services on-demand filesystem unsandboxing requests from native titles and homebrew shells.
required_for_prosperous.unlocks: allow native titles to access /user and /data

required_for_prosperous.name: ftpsrv
required_for_prosperous.why: file access, and the way everything else gets fixed from another machine. Early on purpose: if something later in the chain hangs the target, whether this came up first decides between a repair over the network and a walk to the console with a USB stick.
required_for_prosperous.unlocks: retrieve reports, stage payloads and packages

required_for_prosperous.name: elfldr
required_for_prosperous.why: keeps the ELF loader on 9021 open after the boot chain has finished, so payloads can be sent over the network. LAST, AND ONLY IN THE MANAGER'S OWN LIST.
required_for_prosperous.unlocks: send a payload to the target and run it

capture.label: payload manager settings
capture.why: the manager's own settings file. It holds the switch that decides whether the manager reads its list at all, and whatever else a setup has tuned - the disc-player behaviour, the startup delay. Exporting a chain without it keeps the payload order and loses the behaviour around it, so an exported chain carries a copy and a deploy puts it back. This is a PATH, not its contents: nothing about one machine's settings is shipped here - the copy only ever lives in a chain somebody exported off their own console.

presets.name: payload-manager
presets.about: The two-role split done cleanly: nine payloads in the manager's own list - the loader last, so 9021 stays open - and only the manager itself in the autoloader's list that starts it. Everything is in exactly one list rather than duplicated across both.

entries.name: kstuff-lite
entries.why: patches the kernel so unsigned code can run, and goes first because until it has, memory cannot be made executable and non-payload homebrew and fake packages are unavailable - measured in etaHEN's own loader, which waits for an RWX mprotect to succeed before continuing. ONE KERNEL PATCH, NOT TWO: kstuff and kstuff-lite do the same job and this chain names only this one, because it is the one the console this chain was taken from actually runs.

entries.name: pltauth-patch
entries.why: patches /dev/pltauth so native Prospero (category 0) homebrew passes PFAuthClient entitlement verification (0x80de0051). Must run after kstuff-lite so kernel memory is accessible, and before any native application launches.

entries.name: sandbox-daemon
entries.why: services on-demand filesystem unsandboxing requests from native titles and homebrew shells.
entries.unlocks: allow native titles to access /user and /data

entries.name: elfldr
entries.why: keeps the ELF loader on 9021 open after the boot chain has finished, so payloads can be sent over the network. LAST, AND ONLY IN THE MANAGER'S OWN LIST. Read from y2jb's source: aioshellcode.js maps and starts the loader itself, and autoload.js then waits for it to accept connections on 9021 before it reads a list at all - so by the time an autoloader's list runs, an entry for the loader is a second copy arriving at a port the first one already holds. (This file carried that as a quotation from y2jb's README until 2026-09-02; the repository contains no such sentence, and the source says it better.) This file said the opposite until 2026-09-01, on the reasoning that everything after it loads through it; that is true, and it is the autoloader's job rather than the list's. In the manager's own list it belongs last: elfldr's lifetime is the boot chain, so by the time that list has run the first one has exited, and this is what puts one back and leaves it up. THIS IS A DEVELOPMENT CHOICE, NOT A REPAIR: a console that answers nothing on 9021 after boot is working correctly.

entries.name: nanoDNS
entries.why: no ordering requirement: it serves DNS and nothing in a startup chain waits on it.
entries.unlocks: block telemetry and firmware updates via DNS

entries.name: ShadowMountPlus
entries.why: mounts content in the background and needs the kernel patched first, so it belongs after kstuff. Nothing else waits on it.

entries.name: ps5upload
entries.why: no ordering requirement: it is a transfer service, and nothing in a startup chain waits on it.
entries.unlocks: transfer payloads and files at high speed

entries.name: ftpsrv
entries.why: file access, and the way everything else gets fixed from another machine. Early on purpose: if something later in the chain hangs the target, whether this came up first decides between a repair over the network and a walk to the console with a USB stick.
entries.unlocks: retrieve reports, stage payloads and packages

entries.name: klogsrv
entries.why: the system log. Nothing depends on it and it depends on nothing, so its position is free - but it is placed before the payloads that might fail, because a log started afterwards cannot say why they did.

entries.name: shsrv
entries.why: a shell, and the second way back in. It can run a payload already on the target's disk, so it is what remains when the loader is the thing that broke.

entries.name: pldmgr
entries.why: the payload manager, and it goes LAST in an autoloader's list. It runs a startup list of its own once it is up, so anything the autoloader is going to do should be done before it starts. An autoloader list that omits it never starts it - and the manager's own list then never runs, silently.

presets.result: A console that comes back after every restart with: unsigned code allowed to run, a DNS proxy, background content mounting, fast transfers from your machine, a file server on 2121, the kernel log readable on 3232, a shell on 2323, and the ELF loader on 9021 still listening afterwards so payloads can be sent ad hoc. Everything is a separate payload, so any one of them can be replaced or dropped without touching the others - and any one of them going wrong leaves the rest standing.

presets.name: etaHEN
presets.about: One payload that contains most of the others. etaHEN embeds kstuff, serves the loader on 9021, and brings up FTP, klog and the package installer itself - so listing those separately is at best redundant and at worst a second copy fighting the first for a port.

entries.name: etaHEN
entries.why: brings up the jailbreak daemon and loads kstuff itself, then serves the loader on 9021 and starts FTP, the kernel log and the package installer. When it is present it is what establishes the environment everything else assumes, so nothing may precede it - and the payloads it already contains must not be listed again beside it.
entries.unlocks: run the jailbreak daemon, kernel patch and servers

entries.name: ShadowMountPlus
entries.why: mounts content in the background and needs the kernel patched first, which etaHEN has done by this point. Not part of etaHEN, so it is listed.

entries.name: pldmgr
entries.why: the payload manager, LAST as always - it runs a startup list of its own once it is up, so anything this list is going to do should be done before it starts. Optional under etaHEN, which has its own way of loading payloads; listed here for somebody who wants both.

presets.result: A console brought up by one payload rather than a dozen. etaHEN patches the kernel, then serves the ELF loader, an FTP server, the kernel log and a package installer itself - so after a restart those are running and there is nothing separate to keep in step with them. Fewer moving parts and one version to track, at the cost of not being able to replace any single piece: if etaHEN's FTP server is not the one you want, the answer is a different chain rather than a different payload.
